A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cross-snapshot crosscoder study. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original crosscoder reconstruction experiments, feature-evolution measurements, linear-probe results and downstream-task ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds random-feature controls and experiments across model initializations, model families, training corpora and checkpoint selections.

M1.justification: The cross-snapshot encoder, snapshot-specific decoders, JumpReLU activation, sparsity penalties and integrated-gradient attribution procedure are unchanged. The additional experiments apply the existing method.

E1.justification: Appendix G.2 adds crosscoder training and analysis on FineWeb-Edu, representing educational webpages, alongside the retained SlimPajama corpus. This is a limited corpus/domain extension; the induction, subject-verb agreement and indirect-object identification tasks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Appendix E.5 and Figure 20 add random-feature selection as a comparator for attribution-ranked selection on Across-PP subject-verb agreement, testing removal and preservation of 15, 80 and 300 features. The per-snapshot SAE comparison already existed in v1.

E3.justification: The added experiments use 24,576-feature layer-6 crosscoders on additional base-model configurations, introduce matched-size random controls, and test 16 checkpoints selected from the original 32 by taking every other checkpoint. These are targeted protocol extensions; the original training settings, Table 1 hyperparameters and downstream evaluation procedures are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing layer, dictionary-size and feature-ablation analyses, v2 adds a substantial robustness suite. Appendices E.5 and G test whether attribution outperforms random selection and whether feature-evolution findings persist across initializations, GPT-2, educational web text and reduced checkpoint density.

E5.justification: Appendix G.1 explicitly analyzes two additional Pythia-160M pretraining seeds, adding cross-initialization replication absent from v1. Results are shown separately without new aggregate uncertainty estimates or significance tests; the existing correlation statistics remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Existing results are retained, including the complexity correlation r = 0.309, p = 0.002. Figures 20 and 26–33 add substantial empirical findings: attribution-ranked features outperform random selections, and broad evolution patterns recur under the added conditions. GPT-2 additionally shows later initialization-feature peaks and weak performance recovery when only selected features are preserved in Figure 31c.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives and attribution equations are retained, with no new theorem, proof or derivation. Section 6 changes the normalized-vector subscript in the explanation of Equation 6 from j to i; this is a notation correction without a changed formula.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about tracking feature evolution, later emergence of complex features, downstream causal connections and two-stage learning. The additional evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix G adds interpretations of generalizability and explains GPT-2's different initialization-feature trajectory through absolute positional embeddings and activation normalization. It also identifies insufficient or insufficiently early checkpoints as obstacles to studying BLOOM and OLMo. The alignment-failure discussion moved into Section 3 was already present in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access statement and a reproducibility statement identifying the implementation and a specific reproduction README. Appendix G supplies the additional model identifier and newly discloses normalization of activation sources to average norm sqrt(d_model). The detailed original training instructions and hyperparameter table are retained.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds citations to Svete and Cotterell, Nguyen, and Chen et al.; Appendix G adds sources for Polypythias, FineWeb, BLOOM and OLMo. These extend supporting context without substantially revising the related-work framework or novelty claim.

P1.justification: The SAE-comparison and alignment-failure discussions move from Appendices A.5–A.6 into Section 3. v2 also adds reproducibility and LLM-use statements and reorganizes the appendices, while retaining most existing prose and the main section sequence.

P2.justification: The graphical presentation expands substantially with the random-control comparison in Figure 20 and the model, seed, corpus and checkpoint analyses in Figures 26–33. The existing SAE comparison is additionally displayed in the main text as Figure 3 while remaining as Figure 9 in the appendix. Earlier plots and Table 1 are retained, with relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: The new random-feature control and generalizability tests address dependencies left untested in v1, while concrete reproduction instructions improve reproducibility. These provide useful additional support for the existing findings. The gains remain bounded: seed replication lacks aggregate uncertainty estimates, and GPT-2's weak selected-feature-only recovery in Figure 31c limits the added evidence for general task sufficiency.
